newsitem.title: USA: Navigational problem crops up on U.S. shuttle mission.
newsitem.headline: Navigational problem crops up on U.S. shuttle mission.

text.p: Shuttle Columbia's crew successfully reeled in an orbiting telescope on Wednesday, but faced a fresh technical problem when one of the orbiter's three navigation units unexpectedly shut down.

Last weekend, the astronauts' attempt to make a pair of lengthy spacewalks was scrapped when an airlock hatch stubbornly remained closed. NASA engineers have been stumped by the hatch problem, which occurred for the first time in the shuttle's 15-year history.

Another equipment problem, this time with a navigational tool known as an inertial measurement unit, arose early on Wednesday as ground controllers were studying whether to call the shuttle home one day early. Rainy weather was forecast for the shuttle's landing site at Kennedy Space Centre in Florida on Friday, and high winds were expected at two alternative sites on the U.S. West Coast.
Space agency officials were to meet at 8 a.m. EST (1300 GMT) to decide whether to bring the crew home on Thursday or Friday.

A Thursday landing would be in line with NASA's original flight plan for the mission. Controllers earlier this week gave the crew the green light to remain in orbit an extra day to do more troubleshooting of the stuck hatch.

Although a navigational problem would ordinarily force a shuttle to cut short its mission, Columbia is equipped with two other navigational units and the problem was not considered life-threatening, a NASA spokesman said.
Earlier on Wednesday, astronauts aboard the Columbia guided the shuttle through a tricky manoeuvre to retrieve an orbiting telescope.

Through a series of precise rocket burns and careful steering, the five-member crew flew within 40 feet (12 metres) of the Orfeus-Spas, a powerful German-made space telescope. The telescope had been flying in formation with Columbia since the crew released it on Nov. 19, shortly after the shuttle was launched from Kennedy Space Centre.
Astronauts Tom Jones and Tammy Jernigan used the shuttle's robot arm to slowly pluck the satellite from space at 3:26 a.m. EST (0826 GMT) and tuck it into the payload bay for the ride home.

Scientists on the ground hope to collect data from the ultra-violet telescope to learn more about the life cycle of stars, especially the gaseous, soupy matter that acts as a nursery for stars outside the earth's solar system.

"The entire crew has been fascinated by all the observations," Jernigan said, referring to the telescope data collected. "We appreciate all the information you've sent us on all of the stars and galaxies and interstellar medium observations that have been performed. We think their observatory will undoubtedly make new discoveries."
German high school students have already been analysing some of the data transmitted by the telescope, performing studies similar to that of some professional astronomers, she said.

In what was an unusually busy night for NASA, the astronauts reeled in the telescope just an hour after a separate team of space agency scientists successfully launched an unmanned Mars Pathfinder probe aboard a Delta 2 rocket from Cape Canaveral. The probe is scheduled to land on Mars on July 4 to collect information.

The shuttle's jammed airlock hatch last weekend was a major disappointment of the 17-day mission. The unyielding hatch prevented two astronauts from leaving the orbiter and making a pair of lengthy space walks to test construction materials for the planned orbiting space station.
NASA officials said they were still trying to figure out the cause of the problem.
